title: Pathology-Free Real-Space Renormalization Group Theory on an Inverse Limit Space
abstract: It has been over fifty years since Kenneth Wilson had his Nobel-prize-winning ideas on the renormalization group. In this time frame, despite many attempts, no mathematical results have implemented Wilson's vision to a satisfactory degree. Although a number of predictions stemming from the renormalization group framework have been proven to date, these proofs usually rely on alternative ideas and do not cover the full predictive power of Wilson's renormalization group. The discovery of pathologies within rigorous implementations of renormalization group transformations have further reduced the enthusiasm of the mathematics community for this subject. This paper presents a novel framework to implement Wilson's original idea in a rigorous manner based on inverse limits of finite systems. Doing so, one avoids these pathologies and hence obtains a mathematically sound framework for Wilson's renormalization group. This opens up a completely new path to tackle some of the existing problems in rigorous renormalization group theory like the existence of non-trivial fixed points.
summary: This paper presents a novel, mathematically rigorous framework for Wilson's Renormalization Group theory by employing inverse limits of finite systems. It successfully defines a continuous RG map on the space of physical Hamiltonians, thereby avoiding pathologies found in previous rigorous attempts. This provides a powerful new tool to study critical phenomena and fixed points in statistical mechanics.
main_problem: To develop a mathematically rigorous and pathology-free framework for Wilson's Renormalization Group (RG) theory.
main_result: The authors establish a continuous RG map on a quotient space of Hamilton functions, proving the framework's mathematical soundness and providing a path to study fixed points.
method: The core method involves using inverse limits of finite systems and defining the RG transformation on the space of physical interactions ($V_{	ext{phys}}$) to ensure mathematical consistency.
model_or_system: The theory is applied to the Ising model on the hypercubic lattice ($\mathbb{Z}^d$), analyzing the flow of interactions (Hamilton functions) in the infinite volume limit.
key_observables: RG flow, fixed points (e.g., $H=0$), critical exponents, and the norm $\lVert [\hat{H}] Vert_{\hat{V}}$ used to measure convergence.
important_parameters: The decay rate of interactions ($\Phi$), the lattice dimension ($d$), and the coupling constants ($ eta$).
main_assumptions: The framework assumes the existence of a suitable space $V_{	ext{phys}}$ and relies on proving the continuity of the RG map $R$ on this space.
paper_structure: The paper builds from defining block-spin RGTs on finite graphs using inverse limits, establishing the map $R: V_{	ext{phys}} 	o V_{	ext{phys}}$, and finally analyzing the flow properties on the quotient space $\hat{V} = V_{	ext{phys}}/R$.
why_interesting: While focused on classical statistical mechanics, the rigorous mathematical machinery developed—especially the use of functional spaces, continuity proofs, and flow analysis—is highly relevant to understanding the dynamics of open quantum systems or quantum field theories where renormalization is key.
